Situation1: Your friend has misunderstood the tone of your text message and replied sounding hurt. You need to call them right now to explain.
Expectation2: Repair or replace damaged wooden structures or components
Situation2: A customer brings a child’s wooden toy that is broken, and the carpenter should provide a repair quote
Story:
I was sanding down a splintered edge on a child’s wooden toy when my phone buzzed. Glancing at the screen, I saw a message from my friend, Sarah. Her words were clipped, her tone wounded. She’d misunderstood my last text, thinking I was annoyed with her. My chest tightened. I knew I should call her right away, clear things up before the misunderstanding grew. That’s what friends do—communicate, resolve things openly.

But just then, the customer who’d brought in the toy hovered at my workbench, expectant. She needed a repair quote now; her little boy clung to her side, eyes wide with hope. As a carpenter, I was supposed to assess the damage, explain the process, and offer reassurance. I could see the mother’s anxiety, the child’s attachment to the toy.

My phone vibrated again. Sarah was waiting, probably feeling worse with every passing minute. The customer waited too, her patience thinning. I stood there, torn, the weight of both roles pressing in—friend and carpenter, both needing me, both right now. My heart pounded as I tried to decide which expectation to meet first.
